articles.title: HC reinstates bank official sacked without inquiry over hashtag campaign
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir high court has set aside the dismissal of a J&K Bank executive sacked without an inquiry into an alleged #TortureKas.
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Jammu & Kashmir high court has set aside the dismissal of a J&K Bank executive sacked without an inquiry into an alleged #TortureKashmir hashtag campaign on social media, ruling that a financial institution’s managing director “cannot be trusted with the drastic power to dismiss an employee without investigation”.“The President and governor are high constitutional functionaries and, therefore, they can dispense with the services of an employee without holding an inquiry in appropriate cases. But the same level of trust cannot be reposed in an officer of the level of managing director and CEO of a bank,” the single-judge bench of Justice Sanjay Dhar said in its verdict last Saturday.The petitioner, Saadut Hussain Pampori, joined J&K Bank as a computer engineer in June 1995 and rose to deputy general manager by 2022, serving as an officer on special duty to the chief minister from 2016 to 2018 under the BJP-PDP govt led by Mehbooba Mufti.The bank’s then MD suspended him on April 15, 2024, pending investigation into misconduct before ordering his dismissal on July 15 that year under Clause 12.29 of the officers’ service manual.The dismissal followed a report by DGP (CID) based on “credible sources, as also from discreet enquiries”. The report accused Pampori of spreading misinformation about alleged state-backed atrocities on Kashmiris.The court held that information gathered from sources or through discreet enquiries by DGP does not qualify as an “investigation” under Clause 12.29, since the process involves no collection of evidence or recording of witness statements.Justice Dhar drew a line between Clause 12.29 and Article 311(2)(c), under which govt may terminate an employee without the normal procedure if satisfied that retention is prejudicial to state security.J&K administration has dismissed nearly 100 govt employees under that provision.Clause 12.29, the court said, lays down specific preconditions, including an investigation by a state, Union territory or central agency, before an employee can be sacked.Quashing the order against Pampori as “not sustainable in law”, the court restored him to the post he held before his dismissal, albeit allowing the bank to proceed against him afresh.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Mom loses grip on daughter as passenger ferry capsizes with 20 people still missing
articles.summary: A mother describes losing her grip on her 12-year-old daughter as the Cyprus ferry capsized, with some 20 passengers still missing in waters over 1,600 feet deep.
articles.body: A ferry carrying 267 passengers and crew capsized off the northern coast of Cyprus, leaving at least eight people dead and about 20 others missing as search efforts continued Monday. The vessel was traveling from Kyrenia in northern Cyprus to the Turkish port of Tasucu when it began taking on water shortly after leaving port Sunday, according to Reuters. Survivors were rescued from the water and from the overturned ferry as nearby vessels and coast guard crews responded, Reuters reported. Their mother, Ayten Bicer, described the struggle to hold onto her daughter as the vessel overturned. "She was saying, 'Don't let go,'" Bicer told Reuters. "And I didn't let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn't let her go." A suitcase fell on Bicer during the chaos, causing her to lose her grip on the girl. She managed to grab her daughter's foot, but said oil from the vessel made the area slippery and the child slipped away. The search has also been complicated by the location of the wreckage, which lies in water more than 1,600 feet deep. Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman said a ship from Turkey equipped to assist with work on the seabed was expected to arrive on Tuesday, Reuters reported. It remained unclear whether anyone was trapped inside the sunken ferry. Authorities have also begun investigating what may have caused the vessel to sink. articles.title: Putin, Xi reaffirm Russia-China ties amid ‘unpredictable’ world
articles.summary: The Russian and Chinese leaders met on the sidelines of the SCO summit.
articles.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin have reaffirmed their strategic alliance amid growing global uncertainty, as they met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan.

In their first meeting since May, Xi told Putin on Monday that he was “happy” to meet again. He told the Russian leader, whose country is engaged in a fifth year of war on Ukraine, that bilateral ties between Beijing and Moscow have grown “more solid”.

That should continue despite increased “uncertainty and unpredictability in the international order,” he added. China has consistently denied giving Russia material support for its assault on its neighbour.

Xi told Putin that there are “even brighter” prospects ahead for relations between Beijing and Moscow, although “the amount of uncertainty and unpredictability in the international order has obviously increased,” Xi said.

Putin agreed, saying that “cooperation is successfully developing on all fronts”.

The two-day SCO summit in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, marks the 25th anniversary of the regional security and economic grouping.

Over a dozen heads of state are attending, including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, along with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan as a dialogue partner.

The summit takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow’s Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between the United States and Iran.

Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.

Due to Western sanctions over its invasion of Ukraine, Russia’s economy has become increasingly dependent on China. That has seen Western countries call on Beijing to pressure Moscow to end its offensive.

However, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media that the two leaders largely discussed economic relations, and only talked on the Ukraine war “in passing”.

Putin also met with Modi, with the leaders arriving in the same car for scheduled talks.

Modi said New Delhi is ready to work for an end to the conflict in Ukraine. The Russian leader said Moscow was “following the path” towards a resolution, without elaborating.

Peace talks, brokered by the United States, remain stalled. However, reports last week said that CIA Director John Ratcliffe had visited the Russian capital for talks.

Putin is also expected to hold separate talks with Pezeshkian.

Russia and Iran are among the most sanctioned states in the world and have deepened military and economic ties since Moscow invaded Ukraine. Iran has supplied drones for Russia’s ongoing invasion.

US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran. US media speculated that as well as Ukraine, Ratcliffe sought to convey a warning to Russian counterparts that Moscow should refrain from supplying weapons to Tehran.

Speaking in Bishkek after the first exchange of fire between the United States and Iran in a month, Iran’s Pezeshkian said continuing the war was not in Tehran’s interests.

“We continue to strive for a path of agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region,” he told India’s Modi.

Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian, Modi and Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyzstan President Sadyr Japarov.

On top of the 10 members of SCO, the alliance now has 15 “dialogue partners”, including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.

While the bloc claims to represent some 40 percent of the world’s population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with disagreements among members.

articles.title: IMD predicts below-normal rainfall over country in September
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Monthly rainfall over the country as a whole is most likely to be below normal in Sept, the last month of the monsoon season, said IMD Mond.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Monthly rainfall over the country as a whole is most likely to be below normal in Sept, the last month of the monsoon season, said IMD Monday - an indication that the four-month rainy season is likely to end with overall deficient cumulative rainfall, as was predicted earlier due to the impact of El Nino.IMD said Aug, which reported a deficit of more than 16% in monthly rainfall in the country despite good rains in certain parts, was the warmest Aug in India since 1901, recording a mean temperature of 28.010°C.Region-wise, South peninsular India recorded its second-warmest Aug since 1901. East and northeast India recorded their third-warmest, while northwest India saw its fifth-warmest, Aug in 126 years.So far, the country as a whole has reported a deficit of 14% in cumulative (June 1-Aug 31) rainfall, despite ‘normal’ rainfall in July. In June, the deficit was as high as 35%. Out of a total of 741 districts assessed for monsoon rainfall distribution, 312 (42%) received ‘below-normal’ rainfall and 38 districts (5%) reported large deficient rainfall till Aug 31.A forecast of ‘below-normal’ rainfall in Sept may lead to a deficit in overall kharif acreage. Though the sowing of most seasonal crops is almost complete, with a decline in acreage of nearly 2% compared with the corresponding period last year, low rainfall in Sept implies an increase in input cost due to farmers’ spending on irrigation of standing crops.“Spatially, many parts of the country are likely to receive below-normal rainfall, but some areas of northwest, northeast, east, east-central and south-east peninsular India are likely to receive ‘normal to above-normal’ rainfall,” said IMD chief Mrutyunjay Mohapatra.He said “strong El Niño conditions” are currently prevailing over the equatorial Pacific Ocean, with sea surface temperature remaining above normal across central and eastern equatorial Pacific. “These conditions are expected to strengthen further in the coming months,” said Mohapatra, hinting at its negative impact on Sept rainfall.El Niño is invariably associated with a weak monsoon and a harsh summer in India.At present, neutral Indian Ocean Dipole conditions prevail over Indian Ocean, which are likely to persist through Sept.This means that monsoon may not benefit from this climatic phenomenon as only positive IOD helps increase rainfall activities.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Vienna museum diamond heist: Thieves steal Queen Nazli’s $4.3M necklace
articles.summary: The robbers, who didn’t disguise their faces and were caught on camera, remain at large with the 673-diamond necklace once owned by an Egyptian queen, police said.
articles.body: Austrian police are searching for a pair of brazen thieves who made off with a diamond necklace — once owned by an Egyptian queen and worth millions — by smashing a display case at a Vienna museum in broad daylight. But unloading the hot rocks stolen last week from the Museum of Applied Arts, known as MAK, could be their undoing, art heist experts said Monday. “Just like with paintings, it’s hard to sell well-known pieces of jewelry,” said Anthony Amore, a Boston-based art theft expert and investigator. “The Catch-22 is nobody will buy it intact. So it would not surprise me if their aim is to take the piece apart and sell the jewels individually.” Robert Wittman, who once led the FBI’s Art Crime Team and is now a security consultant, agreed. “What I expect they aim to do is pop the diamonds out of the settings and melt it down,” he said. If they do, they will dramatically reduce the value of a one-of-a-kind piece that Sotheby’s auction house in New York sold in 2015 for $4.3 million, the experts said. “They’re better thieves than businessmen,” Wittman said. “What gives this piece its value is not just the diamonds, but the provenance, the history of the piece. They take this piece apart and they’ll be lucky to get a couple hundred thousand, if that.” That’s if the thieves can find a buyer for the baubles, the experts said. “Anybody who knows anything about diamonds is going to know where these diamonds came from,” Wittman said. The robbery bore little resemblance to jewel heists depicted in movies like “The Thomas Crown Affair” or “Ocean’s 8.” The thieves didn’t scale the walls after hours or short-circuit the security system to get inside the museum. Instead, according to police, they bought tickets, strolled in with their faces uncovered and made their way to an exhibition of works from the French luxury jeweler Van Cleef & Arpels. There, the 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds, which once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, was on display. She wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter and Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the future shah of Iran, according to the museum. The thieves managed to get a hammer past security and used it to smash the glass case, grab the jewels and flee, police said. The museum’s surveillance system caught the whole thing on camera, police said. The Vienna State Police Directorate is asking the public to help identify the culprits, whom it described as slim men with dark hair and short beards. The experts interviewed by NBC News said the Vienna robbery is the latest in a string of high-profile heists that have hit European museums, including the theft in October of French crown jewels and other items valued at $101 million from the Louvre in Paris. “The thieves didn’t disguise themselves perhaps because they knew camera placement and quality,” Amore said. “With the advances in security technology, I fear we might see thieves turn to brute force more frequently in the future. Museums must prepare themselves for this, because they are all targets.” Wittman said top-notch museum security requires good equipment, good guards and good procedures. “It’s like a three-legged stool,” he said. “One leg goes and the stool tips over. Obviously, in this case, they didn’t have good human resources. I mean, the thieves were able to grab the necklace and get away.” That having been said, Wittman said he’s confident the robbers will be found. He’s not so sure about the fate of the necklace. “I expect it won’t take long before they know who they are,” he said of the thieves. “Hopefully, they’ll catch them before they melt this piece down.”

articles.title: Amazon rigged billions in ad pricing, lawsuit from states and US watchdog alleges
articles.summary: Amazon responded to the lawsuit, arguing the US Federal Trade Commission "misunderstands" their ad market.
articles.body:
The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and a bipartisan group of 22 states has filed a lawsuit alleging Amazon secretly overcharged more than a million advertising customers by manipulating online auctions it uses to set ad prices.

The FTC and states say in their lawsuit filed Monday that the alleged scheme has likely netted the company $20bn from advertising customers since 2019.

"Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits," says a complaint filed in the company's home state of Washington.

In a statement to the BBC, Amazon "strongly disagrees" with the premise that it misled advertisers and called the suit "misguided."

In addition to advertisers, the FTC, a US consumer watchdog, and the states say Amazon customers have also been harmed as extra costs are passed onto shoppers.

"Consumers are suffering, have suffered, and will continue to suffer substantial injury as a result," the complaint states, prompting swift pushback from Amazon.

"The FTC wants the public to believe this case is about higher prices for consumers. It is not," Amazon said in its statement.

The company's shares fell following the announcement of the lawsuit, closing 2.5% lower on Monday.

Many brands and sellers compete on Amazon to place Sponsored Product ads and Sponsored Brands ads when consumer search for products using keywords on Amazon's e-commerce platform.

Those placements are then auctioned off to the highest bidder.

The complaint accuses Amazon of secretly charging advertisers more in so-called "second price" auctions, whereby prospective advertisers expect to pay one cent more than the next highest bidder for each bid they win.

But in practice, the complaint alleges, Amazon has charged its Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid close to 80% of the time.

The lawsuit states that Amazon's methods were spurred because "it was unhappy about how much revenue its advertising auctions were generating".

Amazon responded by saying the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate".

"Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," Amazon said in its statement.

"Average winning bids fell 50% from 2019 to 2025 on Sponsored Products search ads, and roughly 92% of placed ads are not given to the highest bid," the company added.

Amazon has tangled with the consumer watchdog in the past.

Last year, it settled a case with the FTC that alleged that it enrolled millions of consumers in its Prime subscription offering without their consent, and knowingly made it difficult for consumers to cancel.

Amazon settled the case for $2.5bn, including civil penalties and consumer refunds.

articles.title: In 1903, 110 million tonnes of rock buried a Canadian town in under 2 minutes; much of it remains buried today
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At 4:10 AM on April 29, 1903, the eastern face of Turtle Mountain in southwestern Alberta suddenly broke apart and came crashing down toward the small.
articles.body: At 4:10 AM on April 29, 1903, the eastern face of Turtle Mountain in southwestern Alberta suddenly broke apart and came crashing down toward the small mining town of Frank below. In less than 2 minutes, an estimated 110 million tonnes of limestone, according to the Frank Slide Interpretive Centre, tore across the valley at speeds estimated at 70 to 75 miles per hour, burying buildings, railway tracks and part of the town beneath a huge field of shattered rock. Frank was home to around 600 people, with roughly 100 living directly in the path of the slide. Between 70 and more than 90 people are believed to have died, although only a small number of bodies were recovered. The disaster became Canada's deadliest recorded rockslide, and more than 120 years later, the remains of the original settlement are still buried beneath the rubble. The mountain itself was permanently changed, leaving behind a scar that remains visible today.How a section of Turtle Mountain buried 3 square kilometres of AlbertaThe rock that came down that morning was enormous. According to the Frank Slide Interpretive Centre, the failed section of Turtle Mountain was approximately 1 kilometre wide, 425 metres high and 150 metres thick. It consisted primarily of Livingstone Formation limestone that had formed more than 300 million years ago, when the region was covered by a shallow ancient sea. When the rock mass broke away, it did not simply fall vertically. It accelerated down the mountain and spread across the valley floor, covering approximately 3 square kilometres. The debris reached an average depth of around 14 metres, with some areas buried as deeply as 45 metres.The material varied enormously in size, from fine particles to enormous boulders. Some of the largest blocks were estimated to be around 40 feet across. The force of the moving rock was so great that when the debris hit the softer sediments of the Crowsnest River valley, the ground itself was disturbed and displaced, allowing the slide to spread farther across the valley. For people living in Frank, there was almost no warning. The collapse happened before dawn, when most residents were still inside their homes. Within moments, an enormous section of the mountain had crossed the valley.Why nobody knows exactly how many people died at FrankThe precise death toll has never been established. Estimates generally place the number somewhere between 70 and more than 90, but the uncertainty exists because so many victims remained trapped beneath the enormous rock field. Only a fraction of the bodies were recovered. Depending on the historical source, between 12 and 18 bodies were eventually found, leaving many victims permanently buried beneath the debris. The timing of the collapse may have saved hundreds of other residents. Although around 100 people were believed to be in the direct path of the slide, many of them lay outside the area that was buried. The disaster therefore devastated part of the town without completely destroying the entire community.The collapse was also extraordinarily loud. Contemporary accounts and later historical records describe the sound travelling an enormous distance, with reports that it could be heard roughly 200 kilometres away. Survivors described the noise and movement as resembling an enormous explosion or a tremendous rushing force. The physical appearance of Turtle Mountain changed just as dramatically. The collapse removed a large section of the eastern face and left the mountain divided into two prominent peaks, creating the distinctive landscape visible around Frank today.Why geologists continue watching Turtle MountainThe 1903 disaster did not end the geological story of Turtle Mountain. The mountain remains heavily fractured, and scientists have continued studying its structure and monitoring movement in the years since the slide. Geologists with the Alberta Geological Survey have examined cracks, rock movement and other signs of instability to better understand how the mountain behaves. The original collapse exposed geological features that had previously been hidden, including rock formations and a coal seam, providing researchers with an unusual opportunity to study the mountain's internal structure.A future rockfall from Turtle Mountain is considered possible because of the mountain's fractured geology, but that does not mean another disaster on the scale of 1903 is imminent. Any future collapse would depend on which section of rock failed and how that material moved. Scientists therefore monitor the mountain not because another massive slide is expected at any specific time, but because understanding its instability is important for the communities and infrastructure below. The lessons from Frank have also become important far beyond Alberta. The disaster demonstrated how quickly a seemingly stable mountainside can fail and how far enormous quantities of rock can travel once a collapse begins.What remains of Frank beneath the rock field todayFrank itself survived the disaster, although the slide permanently changed the community. Some residents eventually left because they feared another collapse, while others remained and rebuilt their lives around the enormous boulder field that now dominates the landscape. Highway 3 passes through the area today, winding through and around the rocks left behind by the 1903 collapse. Huge limestone blocks remain scattered across the valley, providing a physical record of the scale of the event more than a century later.The Frank Slide Interpretive Centre, overlooking the debris field, preserves the history of the disaster through geological exhibits, historical records and accounts from the people who experienced it. The site also helps explain a detail that is sometimes lost when the story is retold: the entire mountain did not collapse, and the entire town of Frank was not buried. Instead, a massive section of Turtle Mountain failed in a matter of seconds, sending enough rock into the valley to destroy the part of Frank directly in its path. More than a century later, much of that material remains exactly where it came to rest.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2012, Jacksepticeye was making videos with a shaky mic; years later, he built one of gaming's longest-running channels
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Before Jacksepticeye became known for “Top of the mornin’ to ya laddies!” and huge charity streams, there was a wooden cabin in Ballycumber, County Of.
articles.body: Before Jacksepticeye became known for “Top of the mornin’ to ya laddies!” and huge charity streams, there was a wooden cabin in Ballycumber, County Offaly. That was where Seán McLoughlin started recording in 2012. The setup was far from polished. His microphone was shaky, the internet connection was terrible, and he sometimes had to keep his voice down so he would not wake his family. His first upload, posted on November 12/13, 2012, was not even a normal gaming video. McLoughlin tried a Solid Snake voice impression from Metal Gear Solid 4. Even the name Jacksepticeye had a story behind it. It came from a childhood football injury involving a friend’s glasses, which badly cut his eye and caused it to become infected.The numbers changed after one PewDiePie competitionThe biggest shift came in September 2013. McLoughlin entered a shoutout competition hosted by PewDiePie, Felix Kjellberg, who was then the biggest creator on the platform. He won. The effect was immediate.Jacksepticeye had around 2,500 subscribers before the shoutout. Four days later, that number had jumped to 15,000. By February 2014, he had reached 100,000 subscribers.That gave the channel a completely different scale. What started as quiet uploads from an Irish cabin had found a much bigger audience.“Top of the mornin’” became more than a catchphraseAs the channel grew, McLoughlin built a very recognizable identity around his Irish background. His opening line, “Top of the mornin’ to ya laddies!”, became part of almost every fan’s idea of Jacksepticeye.But his approach also changed with time. He moved away from the edgier gamer style and pushed something called “PMA,” short for Positive Mental Attitude.That shift became a big part of the community around the channel. Instead of simply relying on loud gaming content, he built an identity that could continue changing as his audience grew older.He turned the channel into a full businessJacksepticeye’s career did not stop at YouTube videos. In 2018, he co-founded Cloak with fellow YouTuber Markiplier. The idea came from a simple complaint about gaming merchandise. They felt a lot of it was cheaply made, so Cloak was created as a more elevated lifestyle and “anti-activewear” brand.Two years later, McLoughlin moved into another physical product business. In 2020, he launched Top of the Mornin’ Coffee, using the catchphrase that had already become closely linked with his online identity.Thankmas became one of his biggest legaciesThe most striking part of his later career has been charity. Through his annual Thankmas streams, McLoughlin works with Tiltify to raise money for major causes during the holiday season.The 2021 event became a standout moment when the stream raised $7.7 million in one day for New Story, an organization fighting global homelessness.He later raised millions more for World Central Kitchen and other global NGOs. That is what makes the Jacksepticeye story different from a simple gaming success story.The career started with a shaky microphone, weak internet and a Solid Snake impression. It eventually became a giant creator brand with businesses, a huge community and charity streams capable of moving millions of dollars.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Iraq sentences militia member for kidnapping American journalist, in rare move against Iran proxies
articles.summary: “Iraq's Central Criminal Court has sentenced Amir Rahim Jabar Lazim to 15 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Law," read the announcement shared by the...
articles.body:
"Iraq's Central Criminal Court has sentenced Amir Rahim Jabar Lazim to 15 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Law," read the announcement shared by the victim, journalist Shelly Kittelson.

Iraq has sentenced a man to fifteen years in prison for kidnapping American journalist Shelly Kittelson in late March, the victim announced on social media on Monday.

Kittelson was kidnapped on March 31, when she was targeted by Iranian-backed militias , and released in early April.

"Iraq's Central Criminal Court has sentenced Amir Rahim Jabar Lazim to 15 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Law after convicting him of being one of several armed men who took me hostage in Baghdad on March 31," read her X/Twitter post.

She added, "I am grateful to the Iraqi judiciary for its attention to my case, as well as to all those who helped get me out alive. And, of course, to those who love Iraq as much as I do and try to build a better future for it. Thank you from the very depths of my being."

Rudaw media in Iraq added that "an Iraqi court has sentenced a key suspect to 15 years in prison under the country's anti-terrorism law in connection with the abduction of American journalist Shelly Kittleson in Baghdad earlier this year, a case the US linked to the Iran-backed Kata'ib Hezbollah armed group."

Rare prosecution of Iranian-backed militia member

The development is important because Iraq rarely prosecutes members of the Iranian-backed militias. In the past, members of the militias have sometimes been detained by authorities, but are often released. There is now pressure in Iraq for the government to rein in the militias , after the US encouraged Baghdad to make progress toward disarming the groups.

The militias have been involved in acts of kidnapping and murder for years. In 2020, Dr. Hisham al-Hashimi was assassinated by gunmen outside his home in the Zeyouneh neighborhood of Baghdad. He was a journalist and security expert. Kataib Hezbollah was also behind the kidnapping of Princeton researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov in March 2023. She was released in September 2025.

Rudaw noted that "the Central Criminal Court in Baghdad on Sunday sentenced 'the convict - Amir Rahim Jabbar Lazem - to fifteen years in prison' pursuant to Iraq's Anti-Terrorism Law 'for the crime of kidnapping the complainant - Shelly Renee Kittleson of American nationality - on March 31, 2026, in the al-Saadoun area' in the Iraqi capital, read a copy of the ruling obtained by Rudaw."

He has already been detained since April for the kidnapping. Other men were involved in the kidnapping. Video at the time showed other individuals. An eyewitness at the scene at the time told Rudaw that "three people surrounded her [Kittleson] and one of them grabbed her from behind."

Kataib Hezbollah suspected to be behind kidnapping

Kataib Hezbollah, which is believed to have been behind the kidnapping, is one of the most powerful of the Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. It has been sanctioned by the US as a terrorist organization. It is part of the paramilitary Popular Mobilization Forces.

Its former leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis was killed in a US drone strike in January 2020. He was driving in a vehicle alongside IRGC Quds Force head Qasem Soleimani, who was the target of the strike and who was also killed. The fact that Muhandis and Soleimani were in the same vehicle illustrates the close ties between the IRGC and Iranian-backed militias.

It does not appear Iraq will hold Kataib Hezbollah responsible for the kidnapping or other crimes. Kataib Hezbollah was also likely behind a drone attack that killed three American service members in Jordan in January 2024. It has also been behind attacks on Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Congo authorities report more than 6,000 confirmed Ebola cases and nearly 3,000 deaths
articles.summary: More than 1,360 people have recovered from the virus in what authorities said was an “encouraging” development.
articles.body: BUNIA, Congo — Congolese authorities said Monday that the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history has topped 6,000 cases with 2,911 deaths. More than 1,360 people have recovered from the virus, in what authorities said was an “encouraging” development. The outbreak in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers’ strike and intense population movements. The situation is particularly concerning at displacement sites, where residents already live in extremely precarious conditions. Last week, the virus spilled into two new health zones in the region. The World Health Organization has said it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-16 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. On Saturday, an Ebola response team was attacked on the outskirts of the town of Mambasa in Ituri province while responding to a call to secure a body. Young people armed with machetes stormed the site of the funeral, forcing the team to flee and injuring one member, a representative told The Associated Press. “We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives,” said Floribert Magene, a member of the response team. Bodies of those who died of Ebola can be highly contagious and lead to further spread when people prepare them for burial and gather for funerals. In response to the outbreak, Congolese authorities have mandated that the dangerous work of burying suspected victims be managed wherever possible by authorities, which can be met by protests from families and friends. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment. Last week, Congo began vaccinating health and other front-line workers with the Ervebo vaccine, which was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type called Zaire. Clinical trials are underway to find a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo virus. Although the current outbreak was declared in mid-May, officials believe it had been spreading since February. It has spread from three health zones to nearly 60, with most cases and deaths occurring outside the network of monitored contacts and within communities. Efforts to bring the outbreak under control — from limited public gatherings to social distancing and airport closures — have disrupted life in the six provinces, particularly Ituri, which also has been ravaged by rebel violence. The government has introduced some measures, including installing health and sanitary equipment at some locations, but advocacy groups say more needs to be done to build trust with the community. While neighboring Uganda declared itself free of Ebola last month, the risk of further cross-border spread remains, WHO said last week.

articles.title: More cells being built within prisons to help tackle overcrowding
articles.summary: The government says £110m has been fast-tracked from existing budgets to speed up the building of new cells.
articles.body:
The government is spending £110m on creating more cells in existing prisons in England and Wales as part of its plans to tackle overcrowding.

The money, which has been "fast-tracked from existing budgets", will be used to speed up the construction of hundreds of new prison places, the Ministry of Justice has said.

Existing space within prisons, such as unused office space, laundry rooms and storage areas, will be converted into cells.

The announcement comes at a time of crisis for the prison system, which is close to maximum capacity, with the government being criticised for its handling of an early release scheme.

Lord Chancellor and Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the government would be "getting spades in the ground quicker to deliver thousands more places to lock up dangerous criminals and keep the public safe".

Norris said: "This government is serious about fixing the broken prison system we inherited, which is why we've already delivered more than 3,200 prison places in just two years.

"We're now investing to boost these efforts further."

Investment to create more prison spaces was announced as part of the government's 2025 spending review, which covered plans for the period from 2024‑25 to 2029‑30.

As part of this, it allocated a £7bn capital investment to create 14,000 prison places by 2031.

The £110m announced on Monday is not a new investment, and is being drawn from money previously announced.

The Lord Chancellor will update Parliament on Tuesday, setting out changes to upcoming sentencing reforms which will block hundreds more dangerous offenders from earlier release.

Measures also include plans to remove foreign national offenders more quickly, and ending the historic injustice of Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences in a way that balances fairness and public safety, the government has said.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said: "It is absurd for Labour to talk about a 'prison building boom' when there are 700 fewer prison places than a year ago.

"In a matter of weeks thousands of dangerous criminals will be released onto our streets thanks to Andy Burnham, including perpetrators of some of the most vile crimes."

An extra £18.9m investment into vital services for victims will also be announced to Parliament.

The services will provide the specialist emotional and practical support needed to help victims move on with their lives, according to the Ministry of Justice (MoJ).

This money will be reprioritised from existing budgets and will be on top of the £550m already announced by government for this support.

The MoJ also announced that it had signed a contract to start building a new jail for 1,700 hundred inmates in Lancashire.

On Monday, the Conservatives warned that dangerous criminals could be freed under the government's early release scheme, which aims to reduce overcrowding in prisons in England and Wales.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said at the weekend that anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the early prisoner release scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.

Burnham said prison space would be found by releasing some inmates serving IPPs as well as by deporting foreign prisoners.

Some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being released in tranches from October.

The numbers due to be released has been reduced after the government said rapists, those found guilty of serious child sex offences and grooming offences and now those found guilty of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme.

Timothy told the BBC that to prevent one group of dangerous criminals being released early, Burnham was "looking at releasing a different group of dangerous prisoners".

Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones told the BBC: "We will do nothing that would risk the public or put the public at danger."

articles.title: Uniqlo, Muji: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
articles.summary: Japanese companies are doubling down on India amid a shrinking domestic market and rising risks in China.
articles.body:
India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent.

If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India.

Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding.

Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai.

It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets.

MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector.

Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake.

Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific.

More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report . GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs.

"Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200mn fund in India, told the BBC.

At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says.

"Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited."

Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth.

Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago.

After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.

But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle.

At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments through some 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. And Goyal has said Japan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country.

Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal.

Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India.

The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently , is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India".

But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC.

India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says.

"With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides."

For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time.

India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai.

But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts.

"Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll .

"Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China."

Also, India remains a tough country to do business.

Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese.

An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed .

Chinese state media was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts.

It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.

articles.title: The Rudan Brothers surprise elderly Canadian couple with free roof repair, then transform entire home after discovering wife is battling two forms of cancer and preparing for chemotherapy
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A roofing team’s decision to repair a damaged roof for free turned into an extraordinary act of kindness after the brothers behind the project discove.
articles.body: A roofing team’s decision to repair a damaged roof for free turned into an extraordinary act of kindness after the brothers behind the project discovered that the homeowner’s wife was battling cancer and was about to begin chemotherapy.The Rudan Brothers, known for taking on home-improvement projects for families in need, initially arrived at the home of Hubert and Anne in Stoville, Canada, intending to repair a badly damaged roof. But after meeting the couple and learning about their difficult circumstances, the brothers decided that fixing the roof would not be enough.What followed was a sprawling home transformation involving a new roof, siding, gutters, soffits, fascia, a rebuilt porch, a new deck, a brand-new shed and several other improvements, all carried out with help from neighbours, friends and members of the local community.‘I have two forms of cancer. And I’m starting chemo very soon’The brothers said they had been looking for a family whose home they could improve at no cost when they received an email about Hubert’s house.When they arrived, they noticed a large tarp covering part of the roof. Hubert explained that the roof had been leaking but that he could not afford to repair it immediately.“We are roofers and we like to offer to fix your roof completely free,” one of the brothers told him in their YouTube video.Hubert was stunned by the offer and went inside to tell Anne. It was during their conversations with the couple that the brothers learned just how serious the family’s situation was.Anne revealed that she was battling two forms of cancer and was preparing to begin chemotherapy.“I have two forms of cancer. And I’m starting chemo very soon,” she said.The revelation deeply affected the brothers and strengthened their determination to do more for the couple.The roof was in worse shape than expectedOnce the team got onto the roof, they discovered severely deteriorated shingles that were so old they could be pulled away by hand.They removed the ageing roofing materials and found that several sheets of plywood also needed to be replaced. They also had to deal with an unused chimney, which Hubert wanted removed.The source of the leak was eventually traced to an area where an older, steeper section of the roof met a lower-pitched section. Despite the water damage, the wooden decking underneath was largely in good condition.The team installed new roofing materials, improved attic ventilation and added protective layers designed to prevent future moisture problems.But the roof was only the beginning.‘We’re going to transform the whole house’Hubert and Anne initially believed the brothers were simply replacing their roof. Instead, the team told them they planned to transform the entire property.“We’re going to transform your whole house,” they told the couple.The makeover expanded to include new siding, gutters, soffits and fascia. The brothers also noticed that the backyard shed was in extremely poor condition.Hubert had asked the team whether they could save some of the old siding so he could reuse it to repair the shed. Unknown to him, the brothers had already decided that repairing the shed was not enough.They planned to tear it down and build a completely new one.The transformation brings the community togetherAs the project grew, so did the number of people willing to help.Neighbours, church members and friends joined the brothers at different stages. Hubert himself regularly worked alongside the team, helping with everything from cleaning up debris to assisting with the renovation.Neighbour Lynn was also described as being “absolutely incredible” for helping throughout the project.The family’s church community also played a major role. Members not only visited the site but presented Hubert and Anne with a donation from a local charitable organisation.The brothers said the experience reminded them why they take on such projects.“It was one of those moments that reminded us why we do what we do and a moment we’ll never forget,” they said.Anne gets unexpected news about chemotherapyAmid the renovation, Anne shared an update from her doctor that added another emotional dimension to the project.She said she had initially been told she could start chemotherapy within one to two weeks but had asked to begin as soon as possible.“I said, ‘No, ASAP, as soon as possible,’” Anne recalled.Soon afterwards, she received a call from the hospital confirming that she would begin treatment that Thursday, meaning she would start chemotherapy sooner than expected.“One week, God answered the prayers,” she said.The brothers continued working as the family prepared for the next stage of Anne’s treatment.A collapsing shed becomes a brand-new 10x10 structureThe old backyard shed was eventually emptied and demolished.For Hubert, the shed held years of memories. As his belongings were removed, he recalled family gatherings and moments from earlier years.But the brothers had already planned something special.With help from Bob and Dragon, a professional framer with more than 30 years of experience, the team began constructing a new 10x10 shed.The structure was built from the ground up, with a new foundation and framing designed to give the family a strong and practical storage space.The project even extended beyond Hubert and Anne’s property. After neighbours Tim and Vanessa helped the crew, the brothers noticed their gutters were also in poor condition.They offered to replace those gutters completely free of charge.The old gutters turned out to be packed with sand, reportedly because of blowing material from a nearby gravel pit. The team replaced them and continued working on the main house.New siding changes the look of the propertyThe brothers eventually moved on to the exterior siding.Before installation could begin, damaged wood had to be removed and rebuilt, particularly around a window where years of water intrusion had caused significant deterioration.The team then began installing new insulated aluminium siding.The transformation was immediately visible as the new panels went up around the house, giving the property a cleaner and more modern appearance.The project also uncovered another major problem: the back deck was falling apart.The brothers repaired the deck so that Hubert and Anne could once again safely use the space and enjoy their backyard.The final reveal leaves the couple emotionalAfter weeks of work, the team prepared for the final reveal.Hubert and Anne were brought outside and initially expected to see the completed renovation. When the van moved away, they were finally able to see the transformed property.The couple appeared overwhelmed by the result.“It’s better than perfect,” they said while thanking the team.The brothers told them that the work had been a pleasure and that meeting them had become one of the most meaningful parts of the project.“We enjoyed every moment spent at this house. All the work we did, it was a pleasure for us,” they said. “Most importantly, we’re glad we met you guys.”The brothers also promised to stay in touch and continue supporting the couple.‘God’s in it’As the emotional farewell continued, the brothers told Anne they would continue praying for her as she began her cancer treatment.Anne remained optimistic about her recovery.“I’m going to be well,” she said.When the brothers encouraged her to keep believing, she responded: “I know I am. God’s in it.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Bernie Sanders claims some Democrats may want their own Senate nominee to lose
articles.summary: Bernie Sanders claims Democratic donors and party leaders are undermining Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate bid over progressive threats to oligarchy.
articles.body: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., accused a small group of Democratic leaders and donors Monday of being willing to see Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed lose, telling "Politico Playbook" that progressives threaten wealthy interests and the party's approach to Israel as El-Sayed faces mounting scrutiny over his ties to far-left streamer Hasan Piker. Sanders said the resistance extended to people at the top of the Democratic Party and its financial base. "You’re talking about a small number of people who are at the head of the Democratic Party. You’re talking about the donor class..." Sanders said. "Are they less than enthusiastic about Abdul? Yes, they are." GRETCHEN WHITMER ENDORSES MODERATE HALEY STEVENS IN TIGHT UPCOMING SENATE PRIMARY Democratic strategist and former Biden White House chief of staff Yemisi Egbewole pushed back on Sanders' framing in comments to Fox News Digital, pointing instead to the party's need to capture the Senate and El-Sayed's responsibility to consolidate Democrats after narrowly defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in the primary. "Dems want a majority in the Senate. El-Sayed apologized for his comments about the Temple Isreal attack and hasn’t campaigned with Hasan. No one is as caught up in this oligarchy business as Sanders is. Stevens lost. She endorsed Abdul. It’s now his job to win those voters," Egbewole said. RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre rejected Sanders’ defense of El-Sayed in a statement to Fox News Digital, arguing the Michigan Democrat’s record and associations made him unfit for the Senate. "Abdul El-Sayed is a terrorist bootlicker who downplayed 9/11, pals around with a radical streamer who thinks our country deserved it, and whose mother worked for an organization that funneled money to Osama bin Laden to orchestrate it," she said. "His presence in the Senate would absolutely pose a national security threat, and it's no surprise that Democrats are losing their minds at Bernie for propping up another unelectable extremist." HALEY STEVENS CONDEMNS HASAN PIKER BUT RALLIES BEHIND EL-SAYED AFTER NARROW PRIMARY LOSS Sanders, who backed El-Sayed throughout the primary, told Playbook that some Democrats viewed candidates like El-Sayed as challenges not only to wealthy political interests but also to U.S. policy toward Israel. Sanders said those Democrats view El-Sayed and similar progressives as "a threat to oligarchy" and a "threat to American foreign policy and our continued support for the extremist Netanyahu government in Israel." The exchange came as El-Sayed attempted to move past renewed questions about Piker, who campaigned with him during the Democratic primary. Piker drew widespread Democratic condemnation this month after remarks about American Jews and Israel, with critics including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J., Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev. Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed for comment, but did not immediately receive a response. EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER Sanders declined to join those Democrats in focusing on Piker, instead dismissing the streamer's controversies while accusing Republicans and the media of distracting voters from economic issues. "Like every other podcaster in the world, he says dumb things that people should reject," Sanders said. El-Sayed similarly resisted repeated questions about Piker at the Michigan Democratic Party convention Saturday, where four reporters pressed him about the streamer. Fox News Digital previously reported El-Sayed campaigned and socialized with Piker during the primary. "We’re in the state of Michigan. If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you’re missing the boat," El-Sayed said. "This is about affordability in Michigan. This is about seeing a doctor in Michigan. This is about Donald Trump’s disastrous policies in Michigan. That’s what I’m focused on right now." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE El-Sayed also apologized Saturday for remarks he made following the March terrorist attack on a Michigan synagogue. He had said, "Hurt people, hurt people," following the attack, comments that drew criticism from Michigan Democrats, including Attorney General Dana Nessel. "To anybody who feels like my comments may have been hurtful, I’m really sorry. That was not my intention. We condemned that terrorist attack. We condemned it outright," El-Sayed said. "What I was trying to do was offer context for why it happened, but it wasn’t the time for context, and you don’t ever want to trample somebody’s pain." An August Fox News poll showed Republican nominee Mike Rogers leading El-Sayed 51%-47%, within the survey's margin of sampling error, while a subsequent AARP survey also showed the candidates locked in a margin-of-error contest. Fox polling found 91% of Democrats backed El-Sayed, compared with 96% of Republicans supporting Rogers. Sanders urged El-Sayed to keep his campaign centered on economic concerns rather than the controversies surrounding Piker. articles.title: CNN admits error after suggesting US troops abroad would be impacted by Trump's mail-in ballot crackdown
articles.summary: CNN's Wolf Blitzer walked back a comment falsely suggesting U.S. troops overseas would be impacted by President Donald Trump's mail-in ballot crackdown.
articles.body: CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer issued a mea culpa Monday after he falsely suggested U.S. troops abroad would be impacted by the Trump administration's crackdown on mail-in voting. On Friday's installment of "The Situation Room," Blitzer sat down with Democratic Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger to discuss the lawsuit the commonwealth filed alongside other blue states to block President Donald Trump's executive order from March to curb mail-in voting, which was slapped with a 14-day temporary restraining order last week by a federal judge. "The continued attacks that we're seeing from the Trump administration is really just an effort to get people fearful, to get people to stay home, and, in many cases, to eliminate what is a valid, safe, secure way for people to be able to have their voices heard and to vote," Spanberger said. CNN APOLOGIZES AFTER MISTAKENLY AIRING IMAGE OF DOLLY PARTON IMPERSONATOR DURING REPORT ON ICON'S DEATH "And in Virginia, you have a lot of military personnel who totally rely on mail-in ballots if they want to be able to express their opinions," Blitzer told the governor. "That's true," Spanberger replied. "It's members of the military service, of our diplomatic service, intelligence services, people serving overseas in service to our country who get their ballots mailed to them at the various postings throughout the world." FEDERAL JUDGE AGAIN BLOCKS TRUMP'S MAIL BALLOT ORDER JUST BEFORE MIDTERMS However, Blitzer made a "quick note of clarification" at the end of Monday's program in reference to his exchange with Spanberger. A comment I made suggested that U.S. military and overseas voters' ballots would be impacted by these directives. articles.title: Nepal floods: Bank vaults full of cash washed away; police struggle to secure them
articles.summary: South Asia News: DEHRADUN: Apart from searching for hundreds of people missing in the flash floods, Nepal’s police are facing another daunting task of tracing and secu.
articles.body: DEHRADUN: Apart from searching for hundreds of people missing in the flash floods, Nepal’s police are facing another daunting task of tracing and securing missing vaults of at least 20 banks washed away in the deluge and preventing them from falling into the wrong hands. Some of these vaults contain huge amounts of cash and other valuables, officials told TOI Monday.DIG Abi Narayan Kafle said that amid the challenging post-flood situation, the force’s first priority is to look for those missing, but at the same time they need to maintain law and order in the affected areas.“There were banks in Rasuwa, Dhading, Chitwan, and other places that were significantly damaged. Many of their vaults containing cash and other valuable items such as gold were either washed away or got buried under heavy silt. Our personnel are now putting all their efforts to find and secure those vaults. There have been incidents where people broke open the washed-away vaults and stole cash.”The development came after police in Dhading district arrested 29 people for allegedly stealing NPR 92 lakh from a washed-away vault from the Upper Rasuwa area. “On Sunday evening, our personnel managed to secure a vault of the Agricultural Development Bank’s Dhunge branch in Trishuli. The task took them nearly eight hours,” Kafle said.He added the vault had NPR 1.5 crore cash and other valuables, including gold worth NPR 50 crore. In another instance, police secured a vault of ‘Krishi Vikas Bank’, Nuwakot.The police spokesperson further said the force has deployed 7,894 personnel in the ongoing rescue operations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A 19th-century Colorado mining town was abandoned; a German investor bought the entire ghost town in the 1990s and spent decades rebuilding it
articles.summary: US News: Dunton Hot Springs in southwestern Colorado is a rare place where a deserted mining town became a luxury retreat without losing its frontier character.
articles.body: Dunton Hot Springs in southwestern Colorado is a rare place where a deserted mining town became a luxury retreat without losing its frontier character. Founded in 1885, Dunton was once a small mining settlement in the San Juan Mountains before it was largely abandoned in the early 20th century. Decades later, German investor Christoph Henkel bought the entire ghost town in the 1990s and began an ambitious effort to bring its buildings, hot springs and history back to life. The result is ‘Dunton Hot Springs,’ a secluded resort made from restored cabins and historic structures. Its story is not simply about turning old buildings into expensive accommodation. It is about carefully reshaping a forgotten community while keeping enough of its original character to make the past feel surprisingly close today.19th-century mining settlement turning into a ghost townDunton began in 1885 as an unincorporated mining town in the remote mountains of southwestern Colorado. Like many settlements created around mining, its fortunes were closely tied to the search for valuable minerals. According to the MICHELIN Guide, the town eventually emptied as miners and their families moved towards areas with better access to the railway system. By the early 20th century, Dunton had largely become a ghost town. Yet its buildings and hot springs prevented the site from disappearing completely. The natural springs remained an important part of its identity, providing warm mineral-rich water in a remote mountain setting. The town also passed through several unusual chapters before its luxury revival. The MICHELIN Guide reports that Dunton later became a makeshift tourist camp and, during the 1970s and 1980s, was associated with a hippie community. By the time Henkel acquired the property in the 1990s, many of the buildings had been left abandoned.What happened after Christoph Henkel bought the ghost townThe transformation began when German investor Christoph Henkel bought the entire ghost town during the 1990s. Instead of clearing the site and constructing a conventional resort, he and his team chose to work with what remained. ‘Emerald Coast Magazine’ describes Henkel's project as a decade-long effort to restore, reuse and resurrect the old frontier settlement. Salvageable elements were preserved, while historic structures from other parts of Colorado were also brought to the property. The approach meant Dunton Hot Springs was never intended to be a perfect museum reconstruction. The MICHELIN Guide explains that buildings were sometimes taken apart, their logs numbered and then put back together. Some structures were also moved closer together to create a more practical village layout around the saloon. The resort was not trying to pretend that nothing had changed since the mining days. Instead, it created a modern retreat that openly blended old and new.Remains of the original 19th-century mining settlementEmerald Coast Magazine reports that the resort occupies the footprint of the original 1885 settlement and includes 14 log cabins. Some were built by miners in the late 19th century. The Dunton Store, for example, remains on its original 1887 site. The buildings also contain reminders of the town's past. The MICHELIN Guide highlights the old saloon, where a signature attributed to ‘Butch Cassidy’ remains on the bar. Other historic objects have been incorporated into the resort, including a ‘copper tub’ from the town's former brothel. Not everything came from Dunton itself. According to the MICHELIN Guide, the ‘Pony Express building’ now used for spa and yoga facilities came from Colorado Springs, while another cabin was moved from Parachute, more than 200 miles away. These additions were chosen to fit the period, helping create a coherent frontier setting without pretending every building originally stood there.What makes Dunton Hot Springs feel like a luxury hotelAccording to Emerald Coast Magazine, cabins feature thick robes, fireplaces, distinctive furniture and private bathrooms. Major Ross, for example, has a wood-burning fireplace, a king bed and a barrel soaking tub, while the historic setting remains visible through its design. The saloon and dance hall have also become important communal spaces. According to ‘MeetingsMags,’ that the property recently completed a multimillion-dollar renovation that began in late 2022. The work included guest cabins, communal spaces, the Saloon and Dance Hall, and the Potter House. One of the restored cabins, Chuck's, is more than 130 years old. It was updated with hand-hewn log walls, custom furniture, a wood-burning stove and four bedrooms. The renovation was designed to give the old buildings new life rather than erase their character.Present reality of Dunton Hot SpringsThe latest restoration has strengthened the balance between history and modern hospitality. MeetingsMags reports that the three-year renovation was completed in January 2026, with the Potter House among the final areas completed. The result is a place where the remains of a mining town have become part of an entirely different kind of life. Guests can eat in the old saloon, sleep in restored cabins, soak in the same hot springs that helped define the settlement and walk through a landscape that has changed remarkably little. Dunton's story is therefore less about rebuilding a ghost town exactly as it once was and more about giving an abandoned place a second life. What began as a remote mining settlement in 1885 eventually became a luxury hotel, proving that sometimes the most remarkable new destinations are created by preserving what history left behind.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Feeling nostalgic for summer? How to beat the back-to-work blues
articles.summary: Going back to work after a summer holiday can be tricky - here are a few tips to make it easier.
articles.body:
The alarm wakes you with a shock, the summer holiday is over and it's time to face that inbox full of unread emails.

This time last week, life was very different. You enjoyed late nights, lazy mornings balancing family fun and you time.

Even if you enjoy your job, the transition from holiday to work can be hard, particularly in September as the days begin to shorten.

Here are some ways of making the transition a little bit easier.

It can be tempting to launch straight into tackling the hardest task first.

But careers coach Sarah Robinson says it's better to "ease back in" by starting with small, manageable tasks and "quick wins".

"It's about trying to build momentum, because I think sometimes it can just feel overwhelming when you've got a massive inbox," she says.

Counsellor Susan Carr agrees. She says it isn't possible in every industry but where viable "be a bit kinder with your expectations of what you need to do on that first day back in the office."

That could mean spending the day going through emails rather than a full day of back-to-back meetings.

Tara Humphrey, a primary care leadership consultant, advocates keeping her out-of-office on for her first day back.

"It's about hiding, if you can, just to give yourself that bit of headspace."

She also says re-entry into work life can be made easier by a clearly-written out-of-office message, encouraging people to follow up when she is back in the office - that eases the stress of whether you have missed something important while on holiday.

There is an alternative. She recalls a colleague who would simply delete all the emails he had been sent during his holiday.

"He said, 'if people want me, they'll come back to me'."

Carr says it is also worth remembering what was enjoyable on holiday and "whether there's a way of integrating that more into your everyday life".

While it may not be realistic to have a siesta every day, you could try cooking some Spanish food, she suggested.

She also recommends holding on to the curiosity we have when in a new place and trying to be a tourist in our own area.

"If we go away somewhere else... we might be looking at the architecture, visiting buildings, and I think - and I know I'm guilty of this in Manchester - we don't always appreciate what's on our doorstep."

Psychotherapist Dr Joy Conlon, who runs wellbeing coaching service Alive 365, agrees.

"Bring one restorative part of the holiday home with you. This might be an evening walk, eating without looking at a screen, reading before bed instead of being on a screen or just spending more time outdoors.

Rather than treating the symptoms, it may be worth looking at the root cause of the back-to-work blues.

Before, she was a counsellor, Carr worked as a solicitor.

"I was vaguely aware before I went on holiday that things weren't right and I was quite stressed," she says.

"I went away on holiday and then I came back and suddenly I was in floods of tears every day. It wasn't just a case of needing time to adjust, it was a sign I needed a rethink."

But how can you tell between a temporary nostalgia for long lie-ins and genuine unhappiness with your job?

"It probably sounds really obvious," Carr says, "but I suppose one of the signs of that is how long it goes on for."

"It's that length of time but also maybe the intensity of the feelings."

Lying on a sunbed, it can be easy to fantasise about quitting everything and retraining as a scuba diver instructor or yoga teacher, but Carr warns against a "knee-jerk reaction".

"It's about taking time and reflecting on how you might go about making a change."

Book your next holiday – and make it active

It is not just the holiday itself that makes them so enjoyable and beneficial, the anticipation of going also plays a key role, says Dr Mark Williamson, chief executive officer of Action for Happiness, a charity.

And what type of holiday or how long you go for can make a difference to the overall impact.

Williamson points to what he says is "genuinely surprising" research which suggests physically active holidays may be better for wellbeing than simply lying by the pool.

"If you include some walking, cycling, swimming, exploring you're more likely to get back feeling refreshed," he adds.

Another factor to consider is the length of your next break, he says.

"Longer breaks give a bigger boost, but it seems to fade faster, partly because you return to a bigger mountain.

"There's some evidence that shorter but more regular breaks bring more wellbeing benefits. The refresh from five days away may feel not far off ten, but you can do it twice as often."
